After the <a href="/wiki/2010_Moldovan_constitutional_referendum" title="2010 Moldovan constitutional referendum">constitutional referendum</a> aimed to approve the reform failed in September 2010,<sup id="cite_ref-81" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-81">&#91;76&#93;</a></sup> the parliament was dissolved again and a <a href="/wiki/2010_Moldovan_parliamentary_election" title="2010 Moldovan parliamentary election">new parliamentary election</a> was scheduled for 28 November 2010.<sup id="cite_ref-82" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-82">&#91;77&#93;</a></sup> On 30 December 2010, Marian Lupu was elected as the Speaker of the Parliament and the acting President of the Republic of Moldova.<sup id="cite_ref-83" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-83">&#91;78&#93;</a></sup> In March 2012, <a href="/wiki/Nicolae_Timofti" title="Nicolae Timofti">Nicolae Timofti</a> was elected as president of Moldova in a parliamentary vote, becoming the first full-time president since Vladimir Voronin, a Communist, resigned in September 2009. Before the election of Timofti, Moldova had had three acting presidents in three years.<sup id="cite_ref-84" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-84">&#91;79&#93;</a></sup> After the Alliance for European Integration lost a no confidence vote, the <a href="/wiki/Pro-European_Coalition" title="Pro-European Coalition">Pro-European Coalition</a> was formed on 30 May 2013.<sup id="cite_ref-85" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-85">&#91;80&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h4><span class="mw-headline" id="Banking_crisis">Banking crisis</span></h4>
<p>In November 2014, Moldova's central bank took control of <i>Banca de Economii</i>, the country's largest lender, and two smaller institutions, <i>Banca Sociala</i> and <i>Unibank</i>. Investigations into activities at these three banks uncovered <a href="/wiki/2014_Moldovan_bank_fraud_scandal" title="2014 Moldovan bank fraud scandal">large-scale fraud</a> by means of fraudulent loans to business entities controlled by a Moldovan-Israeli <a href="/wiki/Business_oligarch" title="Business oligarch">business oligarch</a>, <a href="/wiki/Ilan_Shor" title="Ilan Shor">Ilan Shor</a>, of funds worth about 1 billion U.S. dollars.<sup id="cite_ref-86" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-86">&#91;81&#93;</a></sup> The large scale of the fraud compared to the size of the Moldovan economy is cited as tilting the country's politics in favour of the pro-Russian <a href="/wiki/Party_of_Socialists_of_the_Republic_of_Moldova" title="Party of Socialists of the Republic of Moldova">Party of Socialists of the Republic of Moldova</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-87" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-87">&#91;82&#93;</a></sup> Shor was convicted of fraud and money-laundering and sentenced to 15 years in prison.
</p>
<h4><span id="Pavel_Filip.27s_government_.282016.E2.80.932019.29"></span><span class="mw-headline" id="Pavel_Filip's_government_(2016–2019)">Pavel Filip's government (2016–2019)</span></h4>
<p>Following a period of political instability and massive public protests, a new government led by <a href="/wiki/Pavel_Filip" title="Pavel Filip">Pavel Filip</a> was invested in January 2016.<sup id="cite_ref-theguardian.com_2016-02-16_88-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-theguardian.com_2016-02-16-88">&#91;83&#93;</a></sup> Concerns over statewide corruption, the independence of the judiciary system, and the nontransparency of the banking system were expressed. Germany's broadcaster <a href="/wiki/Deutsche_Welle" title="Deutsche Welle">Deutsche Welle</a> also raised concerns about the alleged influence of Moldovan oligarch <a href="/wiki/Vladimir_Plahotniuc" title="Vladimir Plahotniuc">Vladimir Plahotniuc</a> over the Filip government.<sup id="cite_ref-Romania_Curata_Deutsche_Welle_2016-02-16_89-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Romania_Curata_Deutsche_Welle_2016-02-16-89">&#91;84&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>In the <a href="/wiki/2016_Moldovan_presidential_election" title="2016 Moldovan presidential election">December 2016 presidential election</a>, Socialist, pro-Russian <a href="/wiki/Igor_Dodon" title="Igor Dodon">Igor Dodon</a> was elected as the new president of the republic.<sup id="cite_ref-90" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-90">&#91;85&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h4><span class="mw-headline" id="2019_constitutional_crisis">2019 constitutional crisis</span></h4>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <a href="/wiki/2019_Moldovan_constitutional_crisis" title="2019 Moldovan constitutional crisis">2019 Moldovan constitutional crisis</a></div>
<p>In 2019, from 7 to 15 June, the Moldovan government went through a period of dual power in what is known as the <a href="/wiki/2019_Moldovan_constitutional_crisis" title="2019 Moldovan constitutional crisis">2019 Moldovan constitutional crisis</a>. On 7 June, the Constitutional Court, which is largely believed to be controlled by Vladimir Plahotniuc<sup id="cite_ref-91" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-91">&#91;86&#93;</a></sup> from the <a href="/wiki/Democratic_Party_of_Moldova" class="mw-redirect" title="Democratic Party of Moldova">Democratic Party</a>, announced that they had temporarily removed the sitting president, Igor Dodon, from power due to his 'inability' to call new parliamentary elections as the parliament did not form a coalition within three months of the validation of the election results. According to Moldovan constitutional law, the president may call snap elections if no government is formed after three months.<sup id="cite_ref-92" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-92">&#91;87&#93;</a></sup> However, on 8 June, the <a href="/wiki/NOW_Platform_DA_and_PAS" title="NOW Platform DA and PAS">NOW Platform DA and PAS</a> reached an agreement with the <a href="/wiki/Party_of_Socialists_of_the_Republic_of_Moldova" title="Party of Socialists of the Republic of Moldova">Socialist party</a> forming a government led by Maia Sandu as the new prime minister, pushing the Democratic Party out of power.<sup id="cite_ref-93" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-93">&#91;88&#93;</a></sup> This new government was also supported by Igor Dodon. The new coalition and Igor Dodon argued that the president may call snap elections after consulting the parliament but is not obliged to do so. Additionally, because the election results were verified on 9 March, three months should be interpreted as three calendar months, not 90 days as was the case. The former prime minister, Pavel Filip from the Democratic Party, said that new parliamentary elections would be held on 6 September and refused to recognize the new coalition, calling it an illegal government. After a week of dual government meetings, some protest, and the international community mostly supporting the new government coalition, Pavel Filip stepped down as prime minister but still called for new elections.<sup id="cite_ref-94" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-94">&#91;89&#93;</a></sup> The Constitutional Court reversed the decision on 15 June, effectively ending the crisis.<sup id="cite_ref-95" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-95">&#91;90&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h4><span class="mw-headline" id="COVID-19_pandemic">COVID-19 pandemic</span></h4>
<p>In March 2020, due to the <a href="/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic" title="COVID-19 pandemic">COVID-19 pandemic</a>, the government called a "national red code alert" as the number of coronavirus cases in the country rose to six on 13 March 2020. Government "banned all gatherings of over 50 people until 1 April 2020 and closed all schools and kindergartens in an attempt to curb the spread of the virus". Flights were banned to Spain, Italy, France, Austria, Belgium, Czech Republic, Cyprus, Germany, Ireland, the U.K., Poland, Portugal and Romania.<sup id="cite_ref-sn1_96-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-sn1-96">&#91;91&#93;</a></sup> On 17 March, Parliament declared a <a href="/wiki/State_of_emergency" title="State of emergency">state of emergency</a> for at least 60 days, suspended all international flights and closed borders with neighbours Romania and Ukraine. Moldova reported 29 cases of the disease on 17 March 2020.<sup id="cite_ref-sn2_97-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-sn2-97">&#91;92&#93;</a></sup> The country reported its first death from the disease on 18 March 2020, when the total number of cases reached 30.<sup id="cite_ref-atr_98-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-atr-98">&#91;93&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>According to the <a href="/wiki/World_Health_Organization" title="World Health Organization">World Health Organization</a>, between 3 January 2020 and 28 June 2023, there have been 620,717 confirmed cases of COVID-19 with 12,124 deaths. As of 11 June 2023, a total of 2,288,948 vaccine doses have been administered.<sup id="cite_ref-99" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-99">&#91;94&#93;</a></sup> Moldova is among the first countries in the WHO European Region to conduct a COVID-19 intra-action review (IAR) upon the request of Moldova's <a href="/wiki/Ministry_of_Labour_and_Social_Protection_(Moldova)" title="Ministry of Labour and Social Protection (Moldova)">Ministry of Health, Labour and Social Protection</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-100" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-100">&#91;95&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="Presidency_of_Maia_Sandu_since_2020">Presidency of Maia Sandu since 2020</span></h3>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">See also: <a href="/wiki/Maia_Sandu" title="Maia Sandu">Maia Sandu</a></div>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Maia_Sandu_at_Batumi_International_Conference,_on_19_July_2021.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d5/Maia_Sandu_at_Batumi_International_Conference%2C_on_19_July_2021.jpg/220px-Maia_Sandu_at_Batumi_International_Conference%2C_on_19_July_2021.jpg" decoding="async" width="220" height="147" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d5/Maia_Sandu_at_Batumi_International_Conference%2C_on_19_July_2021.jpg/330px-Maia_Sandu_at_Batumi_International_Conference%2C_on_19_July_2021.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d5/Maia_Sandu_at_Batumi_International_Conference%2C_on_19_July_2021.jpg/440px-Maia_Sandu_at_Batumi_International_Conference%2C_on_19_July_2021.jpg 2x" data-file-width="3000" data-file-height="2001" /></a><figcaption><a href="/wiki/Maia_Sandu" title="Maia Sandu">Maia Sandu</a> at <a href="/wiki/Batumi" title="Batumi">Batumi</a> International Conference, on 19 July 2021.</figcaption></figure>
<p>In the <a href="/wiki/2020_Moldovan_presidential_election" title="2020 Moldovan presidential election">November 2020 presidential election</a>, the pro-European opposition candidate <a href="/wiki/Maia_Sandu" title="Maia Sandu">Maia Sandu</a> was elected as the new president of the republic, defeating incumbent pro-Russian president Igor Dodon and thus becoming the first female elected president of Moldova.<sup id="cite_ref-101" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-101">&#91;96&#93;</a></sup> 
</p><p>In December 2020, Prime Minister <a href="/wiki/Ion_Chicu" title="Ion Chicu">Ion Chicu</a>, who had led a pro-Russian government since November 2019, resigned a day before Sandu was sworn in.<sup id="cite_ref-102" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-102">&#91;97&#93;</a></sup> The parliament, dominated by pro-Russian Socialists, did not accept any Prime Minister candidate proposed by the new president.<sup id="cite_ref-103" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-103">&#91;98&#93;</a></sup> 
</p><p>On 28 April 2021, Sandu dissolved the <a href="/wiki/Parliament_of_the_Republic_of_Moldova" class="mw-redirect" title="Parliament of the Republic of Moldova">Parliament of the Republic of Moldova</a> after the <a href="/wiki/Constitutional_Court_of_Moldova" title="Constitutional Court of Moldova">Constitutional Court</a> ended Moldova's <a href="/wiki/State_of_emergency" title="State of emergency">state of emergency</a> which had been brought about by the <a href="/wiki/Coronavirus_pandemic" class="mw-redirect" title="Coronavirus pandemic">coronavirus pandemic</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-104" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-104">&#91;99&#93;</a></sup> Parliamentary elections <a href="/wiki/2021_Moldovan_parliamentary_election" title="2021 Moldovan parliamentary election">took place</a> on 11 July 2021.<sup id="cite_ref-105" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-105">&#91;100&#93;</a></sup> The snap parliamentary elections resulted in a landslide win for the pro-European <a href="/wiki/Party_of_Action_and_Solidarity" title="Party of Action and Solidarity">Party of Action and Solidarity</a> (PAS).<sup id="cite_ref-106" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-106">&#91;101&#93;</a></sup> 
</p><p>On 6 August 2021, the <a href="/wiki/Natalia_Gavrili%C8%9Ba" title="Natalia Gavrilița">Natalia Gavrilița</a>-led <a href="/wiki/Gavrili%C8%9Ba_Cabinet" title="Gavrilița Cabinet">cabinet</a> was sworn in to office with 61 votes, all from the <a href="/wiki/Party_of_Action_and_Solidarity" title="Party of Action and Solidarity">Party of Action and Solidarity</a> (PAS).<sup id="cite_ref-107" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-107">&#91;102&#93;</a></sup> Gavrilița resigned on 10 February 2023 and was replaced by <a href="/wiki/Dorin_Recean" title="Dorin Recean">Dorin Recean</a> as Prime Minister of Moldova.<sup id="cite_ref-108" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-108">&#91;103&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-109" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-109">&#91;104&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:2023-05-31_Visit_of_Ursula_von_der_Leyen,_President_of_the_European_Commission,_to_Moldova_P061234-676514.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/76/2023-05-31_Visit_of_Ursula_von_der_Leyen%2C_President_of_the_European_Commission%2C_to_Moldova_P061234-676514.jpg/220px-2023-05-31_Visit_of_Ursula_von_der_Leyen%2C_President_of_the_European_Commission%2C_to_Moldova_P061234-676514.jpg" decoding="async" width="220" height="147" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/76/2023-05-31_Visit_of_Ursula_von_der_Leyen%2C_President_of_the_European_Commission%2C_to_Moldova_P061234-676514.jpg/330px-2023-05-31_Visit_of_Ursula_von_der_Leyen%2C_President_of_the_European_Commission%2C_to_Moldova_P061234-676514.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/76/2023-05-31_Visit_of_Ursula_von_der_Leyen%2C_President_of_the_European_Commission%2C_to_Moldova_P061234-676514.jpg/440px-2023-05-31_Visit_of_Ursula_von_der_Leyen%2C_President_of_the_European_Commission%2C_to_Moldova_P061234-676514.jpg 2x" data-file-width="6124" data-file-height="4082" /></a><figcaption><a href="/wiki/Ursula_von_der_Leyen" title="Ursula von der Leyen">Ursula von der Leyen</a>, President of the European Commission, and <a href="/wiki/Maia_Sandu" title="Maia Sandu">Maia Sandu</a>, President of Moldova on 31 May 2023.</figcaption></figure>
<p>Since <a href="/wiki/Maia_Sandu" title="Maia Sandu">Maia Sandu</a> was elected <a href="/wiki/President_of_Moldova" title="President of Moldova">President of Moldova</a>, the country has pursued the goal of <a href="/wiki/Accession_of_Moldova_to_the_European_Union" title="Accession of Moldova to the European Union">full membership of the European Union by 2030</a> as well as deeper co-operation with <a href="/wiki/NATO" title="NATO">NATO</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-:6_24-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-:6-24">&#91;21&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-110" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-110">&#91;105&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-111" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-111">&#91;106&#93;</a></sup> This resulted in Moldova signing the membership application to join the EU on 3 March 2022 and on 23 June 2022, Moldova was officially granted <a href="/wiki/Potential_enlargement_of_the_European_Union" title="Potential enlargement of the European Union">candidate status</a> by EU leaders.
</p><p>Fighting corruption has been a major government initiative, one also essential to EU membership. On 8 June 2021, Sandu signed off on the creation of an extra-governmental corruption monitoring body after declaring the state's own institutions "too slow". The six-member panel of the 'Anticorruption Independent Consultative Committee' will be co-chaired by <a href="/wiki/United_States" title="United States">United States</a> diplomat <a href="/wiki/James_Wasserstrom" title="James Wasserstrom">James Wasserstrom</a>, includes economists, jurists and journalists and is partially funded by the European Union and United States.<sup id="cite_ref-112" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-112">&#91;107&#93;</a></sup> This was followed by the Moldovan government suspending the Prosecutor General <a href="/wiki/Alexandr_Stoianoglo" title="Alexandr Stoianoglo">Alexandru Stoianoglo</a> in relation to charges of <a href="/wiki/Corruption" title="Corruption">corruption</a>, former Moldovan Prime Minister <a href="/wiki/Iurie_Leanc%C4%83" title="Iurie Leancă">Iurie Leanca</a> was charged with <a href="/wiki/Abuse_of_power" title="Abuse of power">abuse of power</a>, the former President <a href="/wiki/Igor_Dodon" title="Igor Dodon">Igor Dodon</a> was arrested by the Moldovan authorities on charges of corruption for the receipt of bribes.<sup id="cite_ref-113" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-113">&#91;108&#93;</a></sup> <sup id="cite_ref-114" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-114">&#91;109&#93;</a></sup> <sup id="cite_ref-115" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-115">&#91;110&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p><a href="/wiki/Russian_invasion_of_Ukraine" title="Russian invasion of Ukraine">Russia's invasion of Ukraine</a> caused significant economic turmoil in Moldova throughout 2022, in particular due to its reliance at that time on Russian oil and gas, with annual inflation surging to 22% and growth falling from a post-COVID surge of 14% to 0.3%.<sup id="cite_ref-116" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-116">&#91;111&#93;</a></sup> In response to these shockwaves, the <a href="/wiki/European_Bank_for_Reconstruction_and_Development" title="European Bank for Reconstruction and Development">European Bank for Reconstruction and Development</a> (EBRD) put a total of €2bn (£1.74bn) into the Moldovan economy and helped it secure gas supplies, a fivefold increase over 2021.<sup id="cite_ref-117" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-117">&#91;112&#93;</a></sup> As of 18 May 2023, Moldovan Prime Minister <a href="/wiki/Dorin_Recean" title="Dorin Recean">Dorin Recean</a> confirmed that the country is 100% independent of Russian oil and natural gas. He stated that "Moldova no longer consumes Russian gas, it is integrated in the European energy network both technically and commercially."<sup id="cite_ref-118" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-118">&#91;113&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>On 19 June 2023 the pro-Russian <a href="/wiki/%C8%98or_Party" title="Șor Party">Șor Party</a> was banned by the <a href="/wiki/Constitutional_Court_of_Moldova" title="Constitutional Court of Moldova">Constitutional Court of Moldova</a> after months of pro-Russian protests seeking to destabilise the Moldovan government.<sup id="cite_ref-119" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-119">&#91;114&#93;</a></sup> The court declared the party unconstitutional, with court chairman <a href="/wiki/Nicolae_Ro%C8%99ca" title="Nicolae Roșca">Nicolae Roșca</a> citing "an article in the constitution stating that parties must through their activities uphold political pluralism, the rule of law and the territorial integrity of Moldova."<sup id="cite_ref-120" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-120">&#91;115&#93;</a></sup> The party was led by <a href="/wiki/Ilan_Shor" title="Ilan Shor">Ilan Shor</a>, a fugitive businessman who fled to <a href="/wiki/Israel" title="Israel">Israel</a> in 2019 after being convicted of fraud and money-laundering and sentenced to 15 years in prison <i>in absentia</i>.<sup id="cite_ref-:02_121-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-:02-121">&#91;116&#93;</a></sup> President Sandu welcomed the court's decision.<sup id="cite_ref-:02_121-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-:02-121">&#91;116&#93;</a></sup> On 26 June, Ilan Shor announced that he would create a new political party in order to contest the upcoming general election.<sup id="cite_ref-122" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-122">&#91;117&#93;</a></sup> On 31 July, the Moldovan parliament voted in favour of banning the leaders of the dissolved pro-Russian <a href="/wiki/%C8%98or_Party" title="Șor Party">Șor Party</a> – including Ilan Shor – from standing in elections for a period of five years.<sup id="cite_ref-123" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-123">&#91;118&#93;</a></sup> Leader and founder of the party, <a href="/wiki/Ilan_Shor" title="Ilan Shor">Ilan Șor</a>, currently a fugitive of the state, has claimed he will contest the ban.<sup id="cite_ref-124" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-124">&#91;119&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h4><span class="mw-headline" id="Russia_related_events_since_the_invasion_of_neighbouring_Ukraine">Russia related events since the invasion of neighbouring Ukraine</span></h4>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main articles: <a href="/wiki/2022_Transnistria_attacks" title="2022 Transnistria attacks">2022 Transnistria attacks</a>, <a href="/wiki/2022%E2%80%932023_Moldovan_energy_crisis" title="2022–2023 Moldovan energy crisis">2022–2023 Moldovan energy crisis</a>, <a href="/wiki/2022%E2%80%932023_Moldovan_protests" class="mw-redirect" title="2022–2023 Moldovan protests">2022–2023 Moldovan protests</a>, and <a href="/wiki/2023_Moldovan_coup_d%27%C3%A9tat_attempt_allegations" class="mw-redirect" title="2023 Moldovan coup d&#39;état attempt allegations">2023 Moldovan coup d'état attempt allegations</a></div>
<p>In February 2022 Sandu condemned the <a href="/wiki/2022_Russian_invasion_of_Ukraine" class="mw-redirect" title="2022 Russian invasion of Ukraine">Russian invasion of Ukraine</a>, calling it "a blatant breach of international law and of Ukrainian sovereignty and territorial integrity."<sup id="cite_ref-125" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-125">&#91;120&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Meeting_of_the_President_of_Ukraine_with_the_President_of_the_Republic_of_Moldova_in_Kyiv_(7).jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/7e/Meeting_of_the_President_of_Ukraine_with_the_President_of_the_Republic_of_Moldova_in_Kyiv_%287%29.jpg/220px-Meeting_of_the_President_of_Ukraine_with_the_President_of_the_Republic_of_Moldova_in_Kyiv_%287%29.jpg" decoding="async" width="220" height="147" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/7e/Meeting_of_the_President_of_Ukraine_with_the_President_of_the_Republic_of_Moldova_in_Kyiv_%287%29.jpg/330px-Meeting_of_the_President_of_Ukraine_with_the_President_of_the_Republic_of_Moldova_in_Kyiv_%287%29.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/7e/Meeting_of_the_President_of_Ukraine_with_the_President_of_the_Republic_of_Moldova_in_Kyiv_%287%29.jpg/440px-Meeting_of_the_President_of_Ukraine_with_the_President_of_the_Republic_of_Moldova_in_Kyiv_%287%29.jpg 2x" data-file-width="4000" data-file-height="2667" /></a><figcaption>President of Moldova, <a href="/wiki/Maia_Sandu" title="Maia Sandu">Maia Sandu</a>, with President of Ukraine, <a href="/wiki/Volodymyr_Zelenskyy" title="Volodymyr Zelenskyy">Volodymyr Zelenskyy</a> in <a href="/wiki/Kyiv" title="Kyiv">Kyiv</a>, 27 June 2022.</figcaption></figure>
<p>Prime Minister Natalia Gavrilita stated on 28 February 2022 that Moldova should rapidly move to become a member of the <a href="/wiki/European_Union" title="European Union">European Union</a> despite Russian objections.<sup id="cite_ref-126" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-126">&#91;121&#93;</a></sup> 
</p><p>According to <a href="/wiki/Bloomberg_News" title="Bloomberg News">Bloomberg</a>, as the Russian invasion of Ukraine took place, the Moldovan government's computer systems used for security operations along the Ukraine border came under attack from Russia. "As the war progressed, pro-Russian social media accounts spread false claims designed to discredit the Moldovan government, and trolls bombarded Moldovan authorities with thousands of fake bomb threats. In August, hackers breached email servers used by the Moldovan president's office; in November, hackers also published thousands of private messages they claimed to have stolen from <a href="/wiki/Ana_Revenco" title="Ana Revenco">Ana Revenco</a>, Moldova's minister of internal affairs, and <a href="/wiki/Sergiu_Litvinenco" title="Sergiu Litvinenco">Sergiu Litvinenco</a>, who was then serving as minister of justice."<sup id="cite_ref-:1_127-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-:1-127">&#91;122&#93;</a></sup> A sustained campaign of <a href="/wiki/Cyberwarfare" title="Cyberwarfare">cyberwarfare</a> from Russia against Moldova has continued with the war, with "denial-of-service attempts to flood Moldovan government websites with traffic and force them offline. There's also been a sustained campaign of phishing emails targeting government accounts, with more than 1,300 received in early 2023."<sup id="cite_ref-:1_127-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-:1-127">&#91;122&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>According to the <a href="/wiki/United_Nations_High_Commissioner_for_Refugees" title="United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees">UNHCR</a>, since 24 February 2022, more than 780,000 <a href="/wiki/Ukrainian_refugee_crisis_(2022%E2%80%93present)" title="Ukrainian refugee crisis (2022–present)">Ukrainian refugees</a> were permitted to cross the border into Moldova. Of that number, some 107,000 chose to remain in Moldova, the rest <a href="/wiki/Seeking_asylum" class="mw-redirect" title="Seeking asylum">seeking asylum</a> further afield.<sup id="cite_ref-128" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-128">&#91;123&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-129" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-129">&#91;124&#93;</a></sup> 
</p><p>The country has received praise from the <a href="/wiki/United_Nations" title="United Nations">United Nations</a> for its efforts to protect Ukrainian refugees, despite being among the poorest nations in Europe.<sup id="cite_ref-130" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-130">&#91;125&#93;</a></sup> About 75% of the Ukrainian refugees in Moldova have been hosted by ordinary Moldovan families, sharing their homes with their new guests.<sup id="cite_ref-131" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-131">&#91;126&#93;</a></sup> 
</p><p>The government's own efforts have been aided by Moldovans for Peace, an <a href="/wiki/Non-governmental_organization" title="Non-governmental organization">NGO</a> civic initiative to provide help to Ukrainian refugees.<sup id="cite_ref-132" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-132">&#91;127&#93;</a></sup> The <a href="/wiki/World_Health_Organization" title="World Health Organization">World Health Organization</a> has stated that "The Republic of Moldova's authorities and humanitarian entities have demonstrated leadership in responding to the needs of refugees fleeing the war in Ukraine."<sup id="cite_ref-133" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-133">&#91;128&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>On 26 April 2022, authorities from the Transnistria region said two transmitting antennas broadcasting Russian radio programs at <a href="/wiki/Grigoriopol_transmitter" title="Grigoriopol transmitter">Grigoriopol transmitter</a> broadcasting facility near the town of <a href="/wiki/Maiac" title="Maiac">Maiac</a> in the <a href="/wiki/Grigoriopol_District" title="Grigoriopol District">Grigoriopol District</a> near the Ukrainian border <a href="/wiki/2022_Transnistria_attacks" title="2022 Transnistria attacks">had been blown up</a> and the previous evening, the premises of the <a href="/wiki/Ministry_of_State_Security_(Transnistria)" title="Ministry of State Security (Transnistria)">Transnistrian state security service</a> had been attacked.<sup id="cite_ref-134" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-134">&#91;129&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-135" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-135">&#91;130&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:TIraspol_Transnistria_(13954559507).jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b2/TIraspol_Transnistria_%2813954559507%29.jpg/220px-TIraspol_Transnistria_%2813954559507%29.jpg" decoding="async" width="220" height="165" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b2/TIraspol_Transnistria_%2813954559507%29.jpg/330px-TIraspol_Transnistria_%2813954559507%29.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b2/TIraspol_Transnistria_%2813954559507%29.jpg/440px-TIraspol_Transnistria_%2813954559507%29.jpg 2x" data-file-width="4608" data-file-height="3456" /></a><figcaption>Russian soldiers in Tiraspol, Transnistria.</figcaption></figure>
<p>The Russian army has a military base and a large ammunition dump in the region. Russia has about 1,500 soldiers stationed in breakaway Transnistria. They are supposed to serve there as peacekeepers.<sup id="cite_ref-136" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-136">&#91;131&#93;</a></sup> In March 2022, the <a href="/wiki/Parliamentary_Assembly_of_the_Council_of_Europe" title="Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe">Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe</a> recognized Transnistria as "a Moldovan territory occupied by Russia."<sup id="cite_ref-137" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-137">&#91;132&#93;</a></sup> On 24 February, the Russian Foreign Ministry claimed that an attack "on Transnistria would be "an attack on the Russian Federation."<sup id="cite_ref-:012_138-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-:012-138">&#91;133&#93;</a></sup> According to <i><a href="/wiki/The_Kyiv_Independent" title="The Kyiv Independent">The Kyiv Independent</a>,</i> "There is speculation that this is a facade for a Russian plan to invade or destabilize Moldova."<sup id="cite_ref-:012_138-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-:012-138">&#91;133&#93;</a></sup> President Sandu dismissed that Moldova intended to invade Transnistria and called for calm.<sup id="cite_ref-139" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-139">&#91;134&#93;</a></sup> 
</p><p>The Moldovan government expressed its alarm and concern in April 2023 when Russian soldiers stationed in Transnistria undertook military manoeuvres without seeking Chișinău's consent.<sup id="cite_ref-:03_140-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-:03-140">&#91;135&#93;</a></sup> The Security Zone is managed by the Unified Control Commission (UCC) which consists of representatives from Moldova, Russia, and the separatist regime in <a href="/wiki/Tiraspol" title="Tiraspol">Tiraspol</a>. "Between February and April, Russian armoured military equipment moved outside the range of the Joint Peacekeeping Forces. The manoeuvre was not coordinated with the Unified Control Commission."<sup id="cite_ref-:03_140-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-:03-140">&#91;135&#93;</a></sup> On 8 May, Transnistria's envoy to <a href="/wiki/Moscow" title="Moscow">Moscow</a>, Leonid Manakov, publicly requested that Russia should send more Russian soldiers into Transnistria because of what it called "growing security risks" from Ukraine and Moldova.<sup id="cite_ref-141" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-141">&#91;136&#93;</a></sup> Manakov also stated that "As long as Russia's peacekeeping mission continues, Moldova is constrained in any military plans and preparations against Trandsniestria".<sup id="cite_ref-142" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-142">&#91;137&#93;</a></sup> Moldova's prime minister, Dorin Recean, said that Russian troops should be expelled from the region.<sup id="cite_ref-143" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-143">&#91;138&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>On 31 October 2022, Moldova's Interior Ministry said that debris from a Russian missile landed in the northern village of <a href="/wiki/Naslavcea" title="Naslavcea">Naslavcea</a> after a Russian fusillade was intercepted by air defenses in neighboring Ukraine. The Ministry reported no people were hurt but the windows of several residential homes were shattered. The Russian strike was targeting a Ukrainian dam on the <a href="/wiki/Dniester_river" class="mw-redirect" title="Dniester river">Nistru river</a> that runs through Moldova and Ukraine.<sup id="cite_ref-144" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-144">&#91;139&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-145" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-145">&#91;140&#93;</a></sup> On 5 December, another missile fell near the city of <a href="/wiki/Briceni" title="Briceni">Briceni</a> as Russia launched another wave of missile strikes against Ukraine.<sup id="cite_ref-146" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-146">&#91;141&#93;</a></sup> Yet another missile fell into <a href="/wiki/Larga,_Briceni" title="Larga, Briceni">Larga</a> on 14 January 2023 as a result of another wave of missile strikes against Ukraine<sup id="cite_ref-147" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-147">&#91;142&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-148" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-148">&#91;143&#93;</a></sup> and again on the same village on 16 February of the same year.<sup id="cite_ref-149" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-149">&#91;144&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Russia's '10 year plan', written in 2021, was leaked to the international press, involved supporting pro-Russian groups, utilizing the <a href="/wiki/Eastern_Orthodoxy_in_Moldova" title="Eastern Orthodoxy in Moldova">Orthodox Church</a> and threatening to cut off supplies of natural gas with the aim to destabilise Moldova.<sup id="cite_ref-150" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-150">&#91;145&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-151" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-151">&#91;146&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>In February 2023 an <a href="/wiki/2023_Moldovan_coup_d%27%C3%A9tat_attempt_allegations" class="mw-redirect" title="2023 Moldovan coup d&#39;état attempt allegations">attempted coup</a> by a series of Russian-backed actors was uncovered involving saboteurs with military training dressed in civilian clothes to stage attacks (including on state buildings), and take hostages.<sup id="cite_ref-152" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-152">&#91;147&#93;</a></sup> The Moldovan government was to be overthrown and replaced with a <a href="/wiki/Puppet_government" class="mw-redirect" title="Puppet government">puppet government</a>. The plan allegedly involved an alliance between criminal groups and two exiled Moldovan <a href="/wiki/Russian_oligarchs" title="Russian oligarchs">oligarchs</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-:011_153-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-:011-153">&#91;148&#93;</a></sup> President Sandu said Russian, Montenegrin, Belarusian, and Serbian citizens were to enter Moldova to incite protests as part of the coup plan;<sup id="cite_ref-154" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-154">&#91;149&#93;</a></sup> Moldovan intelligence believes foreign provocateurs would be used to foment violent unrest during the anti-government protests.<sup id="cite_ref-:52_155-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-:52-155">&#91;150&#93;</a></sup> Foreign citizens were also to be involved in violent actions. Sandu credited Ukrainian partners for uncovering locations and logistical aspects of the plot.<sup id="cite_ref-156" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-156">&#91;151&#93;</a></sup> In a March 10 briefing, <a href="/wiki/United_States" title="United States">United States</a> <a href="/wiki/National_Security_Council_coordinator_for_strategic_communications" title="National Security Council coordinator for strategic communications">National Security Council Coordinator for Strategic Communications</a> <a href="/wiki/John_Kirby_(admiral)" title="John Kirby (admiral)">John Kirby</a> made public information about Russian efforts to destabilise Moldova obtained by the U.S. Kirby stated the U.S. government believes Russia to be pursuing destabilisation efforts in Moldova with the ultimate goal of replacing the existing Moldovan government with one that would be more friendly to Russian interests.<sup id="cite_ref-157" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-157">&#91;152&#93;</a></sup> 
</p><p>In July 2023, opposition politician <a href="/wiki/Oleg_Khorzhan" title="Oleg Khorzhan">Oleg Khorzhan</a>, a pro-Russian critic of the <a href="/wiki/Transnistrian_Government" class="mw-redirect" title="Transnistrian Government">Transnistrian government</a>, and leader of the local <a href="/wiki/Pridnestrovie_Communist_Party" title="Pridnestrovie Communist Party">Pridnestrovie Communist Party</a> in the breakaway Transnistria region, was found dead in his home on the outskirts of <a href="/wiki/Tiraspol" title="Tiraspol">Tiraspol</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-158" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-158">&#91;153&#93;</a></sup> He had been released from prison for less than a year. Reports suggest he had been either shot dead or stabbed, with other reports suggesting signs of <a href="/wiki/Torture" title="Torture">torture</a>. The <a href="/wiki/Moldovan_Police" title="Moldovan Police">Moldovan National Police</a> has opened an active investigation into his presumed murder.<sup id="cite_ref-159" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-159">&#91;154&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-160" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-160">&#91;155&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h2><span class="mw-headline" id="Politics">Politics</span></h2>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <a href="/wiki/Government_of_Moldova" title="Government of Moldova">Government of Moldova</a></div>
<figure class="mw-default-size mw-halign-right" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Parliament_Building_in_Chi%C8%99in%C4%83u.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/bd/Parliament_Building_in_Chi%C8%99in%C4%83u.jpg/220px-Parliament_Building_in_Chi%C8%99in%C4%83u.jpg" decoding="async" width="220" height="157" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/bd/Parliament_Building_in_Chi%C8%99in%C4%83u.jpg/330px-Parliament_Building_in_Chi%C8%99in%C4%83u.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/bd/Parliament_Building_in_Chi%C8%99in%C4%83u.jpg/440px-Parliament_Building_in_Chi%C8%99in%C4%83u.jpg 2x" data-file-width="2775" data-file-height="1975" /></a><figcaption>The <a href="/wiki/Moldovan_Parliament" class="mw-redirect" title="Moldovan Parliament">Moldovan Parliament</a></figcaption></figure>
<p>The Republic of Moldova is a <a href="/wiki/Republic" title="Republic">constitutional republic</a> with a <a href="/wiki/Unicameralism" title="Unicameralism">unicameral</a> <a href="/wiki/Parliamentary_system" title="Parliamentary system">parliamentary system</a> of government and competitive, <a href="/wiki/Multi-party_system" title="Multi-party system">multi-party elections</a>. The constitution provides for <a href="/wiki/Executive_(government)" title="Executive (government)">executive</a> and <a href="/wiki/Legislature" title="Legislature">legislative</a> branches as well as an independent <a href="/wiki/Judiciary" title="Judiciary">judiciary</a> and a clear <a href="/wiki/Separation_of_powers" title="Separation of powers">separation of powers</a>. The <a href="/wiki/President_of_Moldova" title="President of Moldova">president</a> serves as the <a href="/wiki/Head_of_state" title="Head of state">head of state</a>, is elected every four years, and can be re-elected once. The <a href="/wiki/Prime_Minister_of_Moldova" title="Prime Minister of Moldova">prime minister</a> serves as the <a href="/wiki/Head_of_government" title="Head of government">head of government</a>, appointed by the president with <a href="/wiki/Parliament_of_Moldova" title="Parliament of Moldova">parliament</a>'s support. The head of government in turn assembles a <a href="/wiki/Cabinet_of_Moldova" title="Cabinet of Moldova">cabinet</a>, subject to parliamentary approval. Legislative authority is vested in the unicameral <a href="/wiki/Parliament_of_Moldova" title="Parliament of Moldova">Parliament of Moldova</a> which has 101 seats and whose members are elected by popular vote on <a href="/wiki/Party_lists" class="mw-redirect" title="Party lists">party lists</a> every four years. The president's official residence is the <a href="/wiki/Presidential_Palace,_Chi%C8%99in%C4%83u" title="Presidential Palace, Chișinău">Presidential Palace, Chișinău</a>.
</p><p>After the prime minister and government resigned in 2020 and the president and parliament failed to form a new government, early parliamentary elections were held in July 2021. According to <a href="/wiki/Organization_for_Security_and_Co-operation_in_Europe" title="Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe">Organization for Security and Cooperation in Europe</a> observers, the <a href="/wiki/2021_Moldovan_parliamentary_election" title="2021 Moldovan parliamentary election">2021 parliamentary elections</a> were well-administered and competitive, and <a href="/wiki/Fundamental_rights" title="Fundamental rights">fundamental freedoms</a> were largely respected.<sup id="cite_ref-161" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-161">&#91;156&#93;</a></sup> The <a href="/wiki/Party_of_Action_and_Solidarity" title="Party of Action and Solidarity">Party of Action and Solidarity</a> won 63 seats in the 101-seat parliament, enough to form a single-party majority.<sup id="cite_ref-162" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-162">&#91;157&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<style data-mw-deduplicate="TemplateStyles:r1096954695/mw-parser-output/.tmulti">.mw-parser-output .tmulti .multiimageinner{display:flex;flex-direction:column}.mw-parser-output .tmulti .thumbcaption{text-align:left}.mw-parser-output .tmulti .trow>.thumbcaption{text-align:center}}</style><div class="thumb tmulti tright"><div class="thumbinner multiimageinner"
